bull_bear.body:
- Self-funded ~Rs 35,000 cr/yr capex; moderate gearing; large liquid investments and strategic IOCL/GAIL holdings provide flexibility.
- Risk flag: any further **large debt-funded acquisition** could pressure capital structure and coverage metrics (and hence the rating).
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body:
- **Commodity / oil-price risk** — standalone revenue largely from crude; exposure to crude and gas price volatility (windfall-tax/price-control overhang as a PSU controlling domestic energy prices).
- **Reserve replacement / production decline** — high dependence on mature Mumbai High; moderate new-discovery track record; geological, technological and execution (E&P) risks.
- **Geopolitical** — OVL assets in politically unstable countries; Russia cash-repatriation constraints. (Upside: Mozambique force majeure ended Nov-2025; production expected ~2028.)
- **Project execution** — large multi-year capex implementation risk.
- **ESG / energy transition** — tightening environment/safety regulation; long-term fossil-fuel demand shift.
- **Acquisition risk** — large debt-funded M&A could weaken the credit profile.
bull_bear.title: Risks

bull_bear.body:
- Largest exploration acreage position in India under the Open Acreage Licensing Policy - has acquired the highest OALP acreages through the rounds concluded up to Round IX
- Ability to bring in global technical expertise on its own terms: bp engaged as Technical Services Provider for Mumbai High redevelopment and, on early positive results, onboarded for the entire Western Offshore portfolio
- Risk-sharing engagement with leading global energy companies - ExxonMobil, Chevron, TotalEnergies, Petrobras, Petronas, RIL-bp, Equinor and Shell - for joint bidding and farm-in in frontier exploration
- Reserve replacement despite a mature producing portfolio: 2P reserve accretion from ONGC-operated areas in India of 44.01 MMTOE, a Reserve Replacement Ratio of 1.17
- Strong balance sheet with a Debt-Equity Ratio of just 0.02:1 and Return on Capital Employed of 22.46 per cent
- Integrated group structure spanning upstream, refining and marketing through subsidiaries ONGC Videsh, HPCL, MRPL and OPaL, and associates/JVs including Petronet LNG and Indradhanush Gas Grid
- Deep in-house technology and digital capability - Production Operations Control Centre NETRA, Project GATI AI deployment, R&D spend of Rs 7,444.79 million standalone and grant of 10 patents and 4 copyrights from Intellectual Property India
- Governance recognition - Golden Peacock Global Award for Sustainability 2025 and Certificate of Merit at the 38th Jamnalal Bajaj Uchit Vyavhar Puraskar 2026
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Commodity price volatility in crude oil and natural gas — Flagged as a key strategic risk. Prices are influenced by global demand-supply dynamics, geopolitical developments, OPEC+ production decisions and government interventions, and volatility can significantly impact revenues, profitability, cash flows, project economics and investment decisions - prolonged low prices affect investment viability while sustained high prices trigger demand-side pressures and regulatory responses. Mitigated through market monitoring, stakeholder and policymaker engagement, operational efficiency, cost optimisation, production enhancement and portfolio diversification, supported by a strong balance sheet and robust liquidity.
- Decline of mature and ageing producing assets — A significant share of production comes from mature and ageing assets, where natural reservoir decline, increasing water cut and infrastructure fatigue can progressively affect output levels, recovery efficiency and operating costs. Managing it requires sustained enhanced oil recovery, advanced reservoir management, production optimisation and timely redevelopment, delivered through technology-led interventions, strategic partnerships and technical collaborations.
- Exploration outcome and reserve replacement risk — Key operational risk, heightened as the Company moves into deep-water and ultra-deep-water areas with higher geological uncertainty, technical complexity and substantial capital exposure. Limited exploration success, delays in reserve conversion and natural decline from producing fields can affect future output, project economics and long-term financial performance; mitigated through an integrated technology-led exploration strategy with advanced seismic interpretation, probabilistic modelling and disciplined prospect evaluation.
- Climate change and the accelerating energy transition — Evolving decarbonisation policies, heightened stakeholder expectations and changing consumption patterns may influence the long-term outlook for fossil fuels while increasing regulatory and compliance requirements. Physical climate risks - extreme weather, cyclones, floods and rising sea levels - can impact operational infrastructure and supply chains. Response includes integrating climate into strategy and investment decisions, the Net Zero Scope 1 and 2 by 2038 commitment, methane reduction, flare minimisation, renewables expansion, carbon capture and energy efficiency.
- HSE and asset integrity risk across complex offshore, onshore and processing facilities — Major incidents such as blowouts, fires, hydrocarbon releases, vessel collisions, natural disasters or infrastructure failures may result in injuries, environmental damage, operational disruptions and reputational impact. Managed through an HSE framework covering asset integrity, process safety, emergency preparedness and safety culture, with investment in digital monitoring, predictive maintenance, automation and risk-based inspection; the BRSR adds adherence to ISO 55000 and OISD guidelines and crisis plans for oil spills, gas leaks and fires.
- Regulatory, policy and fiscal-regime risk — Inherent to the oil and gas industry - changes in pricing mechanisms, taxation regimes, royalty structures, environmental regulations and energy security policies can impact profitability, project economics and capital allocation decisions. Managed through continuous engagement with policymakers, regulators and industry stakeholders and close monitoring of regulatory developments.
- Cybersecurity and technology disruption risk — Increasing digitalisation of business processes, operational technologies and critical infrastructure raises exposure to cyber threats, ransomware, data breaches and insider threats, which can affect operational continuity, data security and stakeholder confidence. India's critical oil and gas sector faced an exponential surge in coordinated cyberattacks during Operation Sindoor. Managed through a 24x7 Information Security Operations Centre handling on average more than 2.1 billion events per day, ISO 27001:2022-certified ISMS across 42 data centres, vulnerability assessments, audits, phishing drills and awareness programmes.
- Foreign exchange and interest rate volatility — A key financial risk given exposure to imports, overseas operations, service contracts, equipment procurement and international investments; because oil and gas transactions are largely USD-denominated, exchange-rate movements affect both revenue and expenditure. Managed under a structured Foreign Exchange and Interest Rate Risk Management Policy, natural hedging where feasible, and periodic exposure review through a dedicated Forex Risk Management Committee.
- Supply chain disruption and vendor concentration — Geopolitical uncertainties, shipping disruptions, sanctions, inflationary pressures and vendor concentration can affect procurement timelines, logistics and execution of critical projects while raising project costs. Addressed through proactive procurement planning, supplier diversification, strategic sourcing, inventory optimisation, close project monitoring and enhanced contract management.
- New-energy transition investments with uncertain economics — Expansion into renewable energy, green hydrogen, biofuels, energy storage and other low-carbon businesses is exposed to evolving technologies, changing policy frameworks, uncertain demand trajectories and longer gestation periods. Mitigated through rigorous due diligence, detailed financial modelling, sensitivity analysis, comprehensive risk assessments, continuous portfolio reviews and governance oversight.
- Land acquisition, rehabilitation and land degradation — Identified as a material BRSR issue with negative financial implications - land acquisition and rehabilitation are governed by complex, evolving and state-inconsistent regulatory requirements, and prolonged temporary land acquisitions have in several instances escalated into legal challenges, causing project delays and reputational risk. Mitigated through fair compensation, proper rehabilitation and resettlement, proactive stakeholder engagement and periodic compliance monitoring.
- Legal, contractual and litigation risk — Pending litigations, contractual disputes and compliance-related uncertainties may result in liabilities, cost escalation or execution delays, with implications for financial predictability, project execution and reputational standing. Managed through rigorous contract review, legal due diligence, modern contract management and alternative dispute resolution such as arbitration and mediation.

outlook.title: Guidance / outlook

outlook.body:
- Dual mandate: keep India securely supplied with conventional energy today while building the low-carbon enterprise of tomorrow, standing 'not as a passenger of the transition but as one of its architects'
- Arrest natural decline of mature fields through relentless intervention - global best practices, advanced recovery methods and disciplined reservoir management - rather than accepting production erosion
- Bring in global technical expertise on ONGC's own terms: bp engaged as Technical Services Provider for the Mumbai High Redevelopment Phase-1 Scheme and, on early positive results, extended to the entire Western Offshore portfolio
- Comprehensive Western Offshore programme with bp covering reservoir and pressure management, enhanced water injection, pipeline replacement and major capital projects to improve production performance and asset integrity, with benefits expected from FY 2027-28
- Make natural gas increasingly central to growth, advancing development and monetisation of gas resources (DUDP, North Karanpura CBM, Chinnewala DSF) backed by India's expanding city gas distribution network and stable policy support
- Sustained and intensive exploration programme with expansion of acreage in Indian sedimentary basins - largest OALP acreage position through Round IX, with evaluation of OALP X and XI blocks
- PROJECT DeepX: a specialist taskforce to accelerate deepwater and ultra-deepwater exploration, doubling drilling effort over the next two years in step with the Government's Samudra Manthan campaign
- Share frontier-exploration risk by deepening engagement with leading global energy companies - ExxonMobil, Chevron, TotalEnergies, Petrobras, Petronas, RIL-bp, Equinor and Shell - for joint bidding and farm-in opportunities
- Expand the Enhanced Oil Recovery portfolio as a structured effort to raise recovery from mature fields, with 17 ER pilot schemes approved and further schemes under consideration
- Accelerate digital and AI transformation - the NETRA Production Operations Control Centre as a centralised real-time production hub, and Project GATI moving AI from pilot to practice across exploration, drilling, reservoir management and corporate functions
- 'Net Zero by 2038' strategy for Scope-1 and Scope-2 emissions, framed as an avenue for growth and value creation and backed by a comprehensive investment and implementation roadmap
- Scale the renewable portfolio through wholly-owned subsidiary ONGC Green Limited via both organic and inorganic routes, including the acquisition of OGL One Limited and Ayana Renewable Power through the ONGC NTPC Green joint venture
- Develop indigenous carbon-storage capability, starting with the first Carbon Capture and Storage pilot at the Gandhar Field, supported by a dedicated CCUS laboratory and collaboration with leading research institutions
- Use subsidiaries and joint ventures spanning upstream, midstream and downstream as a strategic buffer against E&P volatility, cementing ONGC's position as India's leading integrated energy enterprise
- Pursue unconventional and frontier plays - Basement exploration, HP-HT and tight reservoirs, and CBM development in the Bokaro, Jharia and North Karanpura blocks
- Maintain capital discipline, operational efficiency and technology adoption at scale as the response to a soft crude price environment
- Capital-allocation decisions sit with a Board of a Government Company under the administrative control of MoP&NG, where the Chairman and Functional Directors are selected by the Public Enterprises Selection Board and Directors are appointed by the Government of India. Board-level oversight of financial reporting and controls runs through statutory Board Level Committees, principally the Audit Committee whose Terms of Reference are framed under the Companies Act 2013, the SEBI Listing Regulations and the DPE Guidelines on Corporate Governance for CPSEs. On distribution, a final dividend of Rs 1 per equity share for FY 2025-26 is placed before the 33rd Annual General Meeting for declaration, and the AGM is also asked to authorise the Board to fix the remuneration of Statutory Auditors appointed by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for FY 2026-27. Non-Executive Directors held no shares in the Company as on 31.03.2026, and Directors have no pecuniary relationships or transactions with the Company other than remuneration, sitting fees and reimbursement of business expenditure.
- Net Zero Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions by 2038, supported by planned investment of Rs 2 trillion to offset CO2 emissions, against annual emissions of approximately 8.8 million tonnes of CO2
- 10 GW renewable energy target by 2030; total renewable capacity reached 2.853 GW after ONGC Green Limited acquired 288.8 MW of wind capacity from PTC Energy Ltd. and took over Ayana Renewable Power through the 50:50 joint venture with NTPC Green Energy Ltd., adding a combined 2.345 GW
- First Carbon Capture and Storage pilot at the Gandhar Field, planning to inject around 100 tonnes of CO2 per day into depleted hydrocarbon reservoirs
- Ongoing decarbonisation levers: methane emission reduction, flare minimisation, renewable energy expansion, carbon capture initiatives and energy efficiency improvements, with climate considerations integrated into business strategy and investment decisions
- Alignment with India's climate commitments under the Paris Agreement through investment in adaptive infrastructure, low-emission technologies and climate-smart planning
- Enterprise Risk Management framework institutionalised in alignment with ISO 31000 principles, covering strategic, financial, operational and business risks
- Information Security Management System implemented in accordance with ISO 27001 across 42 data centres, all certified to the updated 2022 version of the standard, with periodic internal and external audits; a 24x7 Information Security Operations Centre handles on average more than 2.1 billion events per day
- Asset integrity management system with adherence to international and national safety standards including ISO 55000 and OISD guidelines, plus comprehensive emergency response and crisis management plans for oil spills, gas leaks and fires
- Business ethics framework with a Whistle-blower Policy and Vigil Mechanism, an Online Grievance Management System, regular third-party compliance audits and ongoing ethics training, referenced against the OECD Guidelines, UN Global Compact, the Prevention of Corruption Act 1988 and the Companies Act 2013
- Biodiversity management through a science-based approach: comprehensive Environmental Impact Assessments before project initiation, funds allocated for biodiversity conservation under the Environment Management Plan, and conservation plans submitted to the State Wildlife Division and approved by MoEF&CC prior to operations, with habitat restoration, land reclamation and rehabilitation of degraded ecosystems
- Water and effluents management aligned with India's Jal Shakti Mission, covering water withdrawal, treatment and discharge, with monitoring focused on regions susceptible to water stress
- Sustainable and inclusive supply chain: joint sustainability initiatives and capacity building with suppliers, supplier ESG assessments, and enhanced supplier diversity through increased engagement with MSMEs and prioritised local sourcing, in response to evolving SEBI BRSR Core requirements
- Human rights practices aligned with international best practices - fair wages, safe working conditions, non-discrimination, right to collective bargaining, prevention of forced and child labour and equal opportunity across the value chain
- Community development aligned with national priorities such as the National Rural Development Mission and Skill India Mission, with structured public consultations, RTI-based grievance redressal, transparent consent processes and a defined share of profits dedicated to CSR under the Companies Act 2013
- Adoption of prudent financial planning including green financing to support sustainable growth, alongside diversification into renewables to reduce reliance on upstream revenue

outlook.body: ONGC's expansion agenda runs along four tracks: reviving mature offshore fields, monetising new discoveries, building out strategic and downstream infrastructure, and scaling renewables. On the mature-asset track, the Company has moved from conventional field management to a partnership-led production-revival strategy, deploying bp as Technical Services Provider for Mumbai High in 2024 and, on early positive results, onboarding bp as TSP for the entire Western Offshore portfolio - Mumbai High and the Bassein & Satellite fields still account for nearly 60% of production. On the monetisation track, the Daman Upside Development Project (DUDP) was monetised during the last fiscal year and, together with the commissioning of the Eastern Offshore project, is expected to support incremental gas output and improve production as the Company enters FY'27, alongside digital initiatives SANJAI, IDAS and the newly installed POCC and a more pragmatic procurement approach for high-value cost elements such as rigs and vessels. Enhanced recovery is being scaled through the EOR portfolio - 33 ER Pilot/Preliminary Screening reports submitted to DGH up to 31 March 2026, of which 17 ER Pilot schemes have been approved (Phase-I), 11 are under approval (Phase-II), 2 notified to DGH and 3 commercial schemes not approved - and was marked by the June 2025 commissioning of ONGC's largest Alkaline-Surfactant-Polymer plant at the Jhalora field (2,100 m3/day, Rs 534.3 million contract, 14 injection and 26 producing wells) designed to deliver incremental oil production of 0.598 MMT by FY 2039-40, an additional 4.27% recovery from the reservoir. On infrastructure, the ONGC Board has accorded in-principle approval for development of 1.75 MMT capacity Strategic Petroleum Reserves at Mangalore (Phase-I Extension) as a project of national importance following GoI/MoP&NG directives; the Board has also given in-principle approval to form a JVC with the Gujarat Maritime Board for a mega liquid port facility at Dahej (GMB approval already given, FID process underway); and ONGC with group companies MRPL and OPaL is establishing a Petchem trading JV including third-party sales, approved by the respective Boards and awaiting Government approval. Two major projects were completed in FY'26 at a total capex of Rs 13,282.20 million - the Produced Water Treatment Plant at North Kadi (November 2025) and the Part Replacement Pipeline Project (March 2026). Group capital expenditure in FY'26 was Rs 611,308 million comprising ONGC Rs 358,784 million, HPCL Rs 157,050 million, OVL Rs 72,065 million, MRPL Rs 20,437 million, OPaL Rs 1,839 million, PMHBL Rs 133 million and OGL Rs 1,000 million. On the green track, ONGC Green Limited - incorporated in 2024 and operational since April 2024 - acquired 288.8 MW of wind capacity from PTC Energy Ltd. and, through a 50:50 joint venture with NTPC Green Energy Ltd., took over Ayana Renewable Power, together adding 2.345 GW and lifting total renewable capacity to 2.853 GW against a 10 GW target by 2030; an ISTS-connected solar power project for captive use was awarded on 21 November 2025 with the corresponding wind tender awarded on 5 June 2026. Decarbonisation capex is anchored by the net-zero Scope 1 and Scope 2 by 2038 commitment supported by planned investment of Rs 2 trillion, with the first CCS pilot at the Gandhar Field planned to inject around 100 tonnes of CO2 per day into depleted reservoirs. Exploration footprint expansion continues through OALP - 46 blocks are on offer in the ongoing OALP-X and XI rounds (28 offshore, 18 onland) which ONGC is evaluating - and through an MoU with Indian Oil signed 27 January 2026 for technical collaboration and participation in upcoming exploration bid rounds. Petrochemical presence is held through OPaL, MRPL, HMEL and HRRL in a market where domestic demand is growing at 10-12% but profitability is strained by China's capacity build-out.

outlook.body:
- India remained the world's fastest-growing major economy with real GDP provisionally estimated to have grown 7.7 per cent, and India's energy demand grew alongside its economy - the demand ONGC exists to serve
- Crude oil realisations softened through much of FY'26 as fresh supply outran demand; revenue and PAT moderation is attributed primarily to lower crude-oil realisations
- Oil price outlook defined by a sharp divergence between near-term tightness and medium-term easing, with Brent already retreated from above USD 100 per barrel to the low USD 80s; market balances remain structurally tight through 2026 on delayed Middle Eastern supply recovery
- As supply normalises from mid-2026 and expands more strongly in 2027 against a muted demand recovery, the market is projected to move into a surplus of around 4-5 mb/d, placing downward pressure on prices
- A more enduring demand-side headwind from rising global EV adoption through 2030, expected to gradually displace transport-fuel demand and exert sustained downward pressure on oil prices over the medium term
- Closure of the Strait of Hormuz triggered the largest oil-supply shock in modern history, constraining flows by around 15 mb/d; agencies diverge sharply on 2026 demand (IEA/EIA contraction of ~1.1 mb/d vs OPEC growth of ~1.0 mb/d, a spread of nearly 2.1 mb/d)
- Energy companies face a dual imperative - maintain capital discipline during near-term price strength while preparing for a potential supply overhang as markets rebalance; the 'tightness now, surplus later' cycle raises the importance of timing, portfolio resilience and cost competitiveness
- Global energy demand growth moderated to 1.3% in 2025 with low-emissions sources led by solar accounting for nearly 60% of incremental growth; electricity demand growing at nearly 3%, driven by AI-related data centres, industrial electrification and electric mobility
- Gas market structurally complex: global gas consumption growth moderated to 0.8% in 2025; European gas prices projected to surge around 25% in 2026 before declining about 20% in 2027; risks to the gas outlook tilted to the upside
- Amendment to the Oilfields (Regulation and Development) Act - providing fiscal stability, resource sharing and an expeditious dispute-resolution mechanism - described as a bold and welcome step to reinvigorate exploration and production in India
- Many principal fields are mature producing assets (Mumbai High on production for five decades), so holding production close to prior-year levels requires relentless intervention rather than representing standstill
- Group resilience anchored by diversified subsidiaries/JVs across upstream, midstream and downstream, with HPCL delivering its highest-ever combined refining throughput of 26.04 MMT in FY'26
- Overseas portfolio through OVL - participating interests in 29 oil and gas projects across 14 countries (14 producing, 5 discovered/under-development, 7 exploration, 3 pipeline) - with the lifting of Force Majeure on the Area-1 Mozambique LNG project a landmark development

currentContext.expansion: ONGC's expansion agenda runs along four tracks: reviving mature offshore fields, monetising new discoveries, building out strategic and downstream infrastructure, and scaling renewables. On the mature-asset track, the Company has moved from conventional field management to a partnership-led production-revival strategy, deploying bp as Technical Services Provider for Mumbai High in 2024 and, on early positive results, onboarding bp as TSP for the entire Western Offshore portfolio - Mumbai High and the Bassein & Satellite fields still account for nearly 60% of production. On the monetisation track, the Daman Upside Development Project (DUDP) was monetised during the last fiscal year and, together with the commissioning of the Eastern Offshore project, is expected to support incremental gas output and improve production as the Company enters FY'27, alongside digital initiatives SANJAI, IDAS and the newly installed POCC and a more pragmatic procurement approach for high-value cost elements such as rigs and vessels. Enhanced recovery is being scaled through the EOR portfolio - 33 ER Pilot/Preliminary Screening reports submitted to DGH up to 31 March 2026, of which 17 ER Pilot schemes have been approved (Phase-I), 11 are under approval (Phase-II), 2 notified to DGH and 3 commercial schemes not approved - and was marked by the June 2025 commissioning of ONGC's largest Alkaline-Surfactant-Polymer plant at the Jhalora field (2,100 m3/day, Rs 534.3 million contract, 14 injection and 26 producing wells) designed to deliver incremental oil production of 0.598 MMT by FY 2039-40, an additional 4.27% recovery from the reservoir. On infrastructure, the ONGC Board has accorded in-principle approval for development of 1.75 MMT capacity Strategic Petroleum Reserves at Mangalore (Phase-I Extension) as a project of national importance following GoI/MoP&NG directives; the Board has also given in-principle approval to form a JVC with the Gujarat Maritime Board for a mega liquid port facility at Dahej (GMB approval already given, FID process underway); and ONGC with group companies MRPL and OPaL is establishing a Petchem trading JV including third-party sales, approved by the respective Boards and awaiting Government approval. Two major projects were completed in FY'26 at a total capex of Rs 13,282.20 million - the Produced Water Treatment Plant at North Kadi (November 2025) and the Part Replacement Pipeline Project (March 2026). Group capital expenditure in FY'26 was Rs 611,308 million comprising ONGC Rs 358,784 million, HPCL Rs 157,050 million, OVL Rs 72,065 million, MRPL Rs 20,437 million, OPaL Rs 1,839 million, PMHBL Rs 133 million and OGL Rs 1,000 million. On the green track, ONGC Green Limited - incorporated in 2024 and operational since April 2024 - acquired 288.8 MW of wind capacity from PTC Energy Ltd. and, through a 50:50 joint venture with NTPC Green Energy Ltd., took over Ayana Renewable Power, together adding 2.345 GW and lifting total renewable capacity to 2.853 GW against a 10 GW target by 2030; an ISTS-connected solar power project for captive use was awarded on 21 November 2025 with the corresponding wind tender awarded on 5 June 2026. Decarbonisation capex is anchored by the net-zero Scope 1 and Scope 2 by 2038 commitment supported by planned investment of Rs 2 trillion, with the first CCS pilot at the Gandhar Field planned to inject around 100 tonnes of CO2 per day into depleted reservoirs. Exploration footprint expansion continues through OALP - 46 blocks are on offer in the ongoing OALP-X and XI rounds (28 offshore, 18 onland) which ONGC is evaluating - and through an MoU with Indian Oil signed 27 January 2026 for technical collaboration and participation in upcoming exploration bid rounds. Petrochemical presence is held through OPaL, MRPL, HMEL and HRRL in a market where domestic demand is growing at 10-12% but profitability is strained by China's capacity build-out.

risks.risk: Commodity price volatility in crude oil and natural gas
risks.note: Flagged as a key strategic risk. Prices are influenced by global demand-supply dynamics, geopolitical developments, OPEC+ production decisions and government interventions, and volatility can significantly impact revenues, profitability, cash flows, project economics and investment decisions - prolonged low prices affect investment viability while sustained high prices trigger demand-side pressures and regulatory responses. Mitigated through market monitoring, stakeholder and policymaker engagement, operational efficiency, cost optimisation, production enhancement and portfolio diversification, supported by a strong balance sheet and robust liquidity.

risks.risk: Decline of mature and ageing producing assets
risks.note: A significant share of production comes from mature and ageing assets, where natural reservoir decline, increasing water cut and infrastructure fatigue can progressively affect output levels, recovery efficiency and operating costs. Managing it requires sustained enhanced oil recovery, advanced reservoir management, production optimisation and timely redevelopment, delivered through technology-led interventions, strategic partnerships and technical collaborations.

risks.risk: Exploration outcome and reserve replacement risk
risks.note: Key operational risk, heightened as the Company moves into deep-water and ultra-deep-water areas with higher geological uncertainty, technical complexity and substantial capital exposure. Limited exploration success, delays in reserve conversion and natural decline from producing fields can affect future output, project economics and long-term financial performance; mitigated through an integrated technology-led exploration strategy with advanced seismic interpretation, probabilistic modelling and disciplined prospect evaluation.

risks.risk: Climate change and the accelerating energy transition
risks.note: Evolving decarbonisation policies, heightened stakeholder expectations and changing consumption patterns may influence the long-term outlook for fossil fuels while increasing regulatory and compliance requirements. Physical climate risks - extreme weather, cyclones, floods and rising sea levels - can impact operational infrastructure and supply chains. Response includes integrating climate into strategy and investment decisions, the Net Zero Scope 1 and 2 by 2038 commitment, methane reduction, flare minimisation, renewables expansion, carbon capture and energy efficiency.

risks.risk: HSE and asset integrity risk across complex offshore, onshore and processing facilities
risks.note: Major incidents such as blowouts, fires, hydrocarbon releases, vessel collisions, natural disasters or infrastructure failures may result in injuries, environmental damage, operational disruptions and reputational impact. Managed through an HSE framework covering asset integrity, process safety, emergency preparedness and safety culture, with investment in digital monitoring, predictive maintenance, automation and risk-based inspection; the BRSR adds adherence to ISO 55000 and OISD guidelines and crisis plans for oil spills, gas leaks and fires.

risks.risk: Regulatory, policy and fiscal-regime risk
risks.note: Inherent to the oil and gas industry - changes in pricing mechanisms, taxation regimes, royalty structures, environmental regulations and energy security policies can impact profitability, project economics and capital allocation decisions. Managed through continuous engagement with policymakers, regulators and industry stakeholders and close monitoring of regulatory developments.

risks.risk: Cybersecurity and technology disruption risk
risks.note: Increasing digitalisation of business processes, operational technologies and critical infrastructure raises exposure to cyber threats, ransomware, data breaches and insider threats, which can affect operational continuity, data security and stakeholder confidence. India's critical oil and gas sector faced an exponential surge in coordinated cyberattacks during Operation Sindoor. Managed through a 24x7 Information Security Operations Centre handling on average more than 2.1 billion events per day, ISO 27001:2022-certified ISMS across 42 data centres, vulnerability assessments, audits, phishing drills and awareness programmes.

risks.risk: Foreign exchange and interest rate volatility
risks.note: A key financial risk given exposure to imports, overseas operations, service contracts, equipment procurement and international investments; because oil and gas transactions are largely USD-denominated, exchange-rate movements affect both revenue and expenditure. Managed under a structured Foreign Exchange and Interest Rate Risk Management Policy, natural hedging where feasible, and periodic exposure review through a dedicated Forex Risk Management Committee.

risks.risk: Supply chain disruption and vendor concentration
risks.note: Geopolitical uncertainties, shipping disruptions, sanctions, inflationary pressures and vendor concentration can affect procurement timelines, logistics and execution of critical projects while raising project costs. Addressed through proactive procurement planning, supplier diversification, strategic sourcing, inventory optimisation, close project monitoring and enhanced contract management.

risks.risk: New-energy transition investments with uncertain economics
risks.note: Expansion into renewable energy, green hydrogen, biofuels, energy storage and other low-carbon businesses is exposed to evolving technologies, changing policy frameworks, uncertain demand trajectories and longer gestation periods. Mitigated through rigorous due diligence, detailed financial modelling, sensitivity analysis, comprehensive risk assessments, continuous portfolio reviews and governance oversight.

risks.risk: Land acquisition, rehabilitation and land degradation
risks.note: Identified as a material BRSR issue with negative financial implications - land acquisition and rehabilitation are governed by complex, evolving and state-inconsistent regulatory requirements, and prolonged temporary land acquisitions have in several instances escalated into legal challenges, causing project delays and reputational risk. Mitigated through fair compensation, proper rehabilitation and resettlement, proactive stakeholder engagement and periodic compliance monitoring.

risks.risk: Legal, contractual and litigation risk
risks.note: Pending litigations, contractual disputes and compliance-related uncertainties may result in liabilities, cost escalation or execution delays, with implications for financial predictability, project execution and reputational standing. Managed through rigorous contract review, legal due diligence, modern contract management and alternative dispute resolution such as arbitration and mediation.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- India remained the world's fastest-growing major economy with real GDP provisionally estimated to have grown 7.7 per cent, and India's energy demand grew alongside its economy - the demand ONGC exists to serve
- Crude oil realisations softened through much of FY'26 as fresh supply outran demand; revenue and PAT moderation is attributed primarily to lower crude-oil realisations
- Oil price outlook defined by a sharp divergence between near-term tightness and medium-term easing, with Brent already retreated from above USD 100 per barrel to the low USD 80s; market balances remain structurally tight through 2026 on delayed Middle Eastern supply recovery
- As supply normalises from mid-2026 and expands more strongly in 2027 against a muted demand recovery, the market is projected to move into a surplus of around 4-5 mb/d, placing downward pressure on prices
- A more enduring demand-side headwind from rising global EV adoption through 2030, expected to gradually displace transport-fuel demand and exert sustained downward pressure on oil prices over the medium term
- Closure of the Strait of Hormuz triggered the largest oil-supply shock in modern history, constraining flows by around 15 mb/d; agencies diverge sharply on 2026 demand (IEA/EIA contraction of ~1.1 mb/d vs OPEC growth of ~1.0 mb/d, a spread of nearly 2.1 mb/d)
- Energy companies face a dual imperative - maintain capital discipline during near-term price strength while preparing for a potential supply overhang as markets rebalance; the 'tightness now, surplus later' cycle raises the importance of timing, portfolio resilience and cost competitiveness
- Global energy demand growth moderated to 1.3% in 2025 with low-emissions sources led by solar accounting for nearly 60% of incremental growth; electricity demand growing at nearly 3%, driven by AI-related data centres, industrial electrification and electric mobility
- Gas market structurally complex: global gas consumption growth moderated to 0.8% in 2025; European gas prices projected to surge around 25% in 2026 before declining about 20% in 2027; risks to the gas outlook tilted to the upside
- Amendment to the Oilfields (Regulation and Development) Act - providing fiscal stability, resource sharing and an expeditious dispute-resolution mechanism - described as a bold and welcome step to reinvigorate exploration and production in India
- Many principal fields are mature producing assets (Mumbai High on production for five decades), so holding production close to prior-year levels requires relentless intervention rather than representing standstill
- Group resilience anchored by diversified subsidiaries/JVs across upstream, midstream and downstream, with HPCL delivering its highest-ever combined refining throughput of 26.04 MMT in FY'26
- Overseas portfolio through OVL - participating interests in 29 oil and gas projects across 14 countries (14 producing, 5 discovered/under-development, 7 exploration, 3 pipeline) - with the lifting of Force Majeure on the Area-1 Mozambique LNG project a landmark development

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: ONGC's expansion agenda runs along four tracks: reviving mature offshore fields, monetising new discoveries, building out strategic and downstream infrastructure, and scaling renewables. On the mature-asset track, the Company has moved from conventional field management to a partnership-led production-revival strategy, deploying bp as Technical Services Provider for Mumbai High in 2024 and, on early positive results, onboarding bp as TSP for the entire Western Offshore portfolio - Mumbai High and the Bassein & Satellite fields still account for nearly 60% of production. On the monetisation track, the Daman Upside Development Project (DUDP) was monetised during the last fiscal year and, together with the commissioning of the Eastern Offshore project, is expected to support incremental gas output and improve production as the Company enters FY'27, alongside digital initiatives SANJAI, IDAS and the newly installed POCC and a more pragmatic procurement approach for high-value cost elements such as rigs and vessels. Enhanced recovery is being scaled through the EOR portfolio - 33 ER Pilot/Preliminary Screening reports submitted to DGH up to 31 March 2026, of which 17 ER Pilot schemes have been approved (Phase-I), 11 are under approval (Phase-II), 2 notified to DGH and 3 commercial schemes not approved - and was marked by the June 2025 commissioning of ONGC's largest Alkaline-Surfactant-Polymer plant at the Jhalora field (2,100 m3/day, Rs 534.3 million contract, 14 injection and 26 producing wells) designed to deliver incremental oil production of 0.598 MMT by FY 2039-40, an additional 4.27% recovery from the reservoir. On infrastructure, the ONGC Board has accorded in-principle approval for development of 1.75 MMT capacity Strategic Petroleum Reserves at Mangalore (Phase-I Extension) as a project of national importance following GoI/MoP&NG directives; the Board has also given in-principle approval to form a JVC with the Gujarat Maritime Board for a mega liquid port facility at Dahej (GMB approval already given, FID process underway); and ONGC with group companies MRPL and OPaL is establishing a Petchem trading JV including third-party sales, approved by the respective Boards and awaiting Government approval. Two major projects were completed in FY'26 at a total capex of Rs 13,282.20 million - the Produced Water Treatment Plant at North Kadi (November 2025) and the Part Replacement Pipeline Project (March 2026). Group capital expenditure in FY'26 was Rs 611,308 million comprising ONGC Rs 358,784 million, HPCL Rs 157,050 million, OVL Rs 72,065 million, MRPL Rs 20,437 million, OPaL Rs 1,839 million, PMHBL Rs 133 million and OGL Rs 1,000 million. On the green track, ONGC Green Limited - incorporated in 2024 and operational since April 2024 - acquired 288.8 MW of wind capacity from PTC Energy Ltd. and, through a 50:50 joint venture with NTPC Green Energy Ltd., took over Ayana Renewable Power, together adding 2.345 GW and lifting total renewable capacity to 2.853 GW against a 10 GW target by 2030; an ISTS-connected solar power project for captive use was awarded on 21 November 2025 with the corresponding wind tender awarded on 5 June 2026. Decarbonisation capex is anchored by the net-zero Scope 1 and Scope 2 by 2038 commitment supported by planned investment of Rs 2 trillion, with the first CCS pilot at the Gandhar Field planned to inject around 100 tonnes of CO2 per day into depleted reservoirs. Exploration footprint expansion continues through OALP - 46 blocks are on offer in the ongoing OALP-X and XI rounds (28 offshore, 18 onland) which ONGC is evaluating - and through an MoU with Indian Oil signed 27 January 2026 for technical collaboration and participation in upcoming exploration bid rounds. Petrochemical presence is held through OPaL, MRPL, HMEL and HRRL in a market where domestic demand is growing at 10-12% but profitability is strained by China's capacity build-out.

moat.body:
- Largest exploration acreage position in India under the Open Acreage Licensing Policy - has acquired the highest OALP acreages through the rounds concluded up to Round IX
- Ability to bring in global technical expertise on its own terms: bp engaged as Technical Services Provider for Mumbai High redevelopment and, on early positive results, onboarded for the entire Western Offshore portfolio

- Integrated group structure spanning upstream, refining and marketing through subsidiaries ONGC Videsh, HPCL, MRPL and OPaL, and associates/JVs including Petronet LNG and Indradhanush Gas Grid
- Deep in-house technology and digital capability - Production Operations Control Centre NETRA, Project GATI AI deployment, R&D spend of Rs 7,444.79 million standalone and grant of 10 patents and 4 copyrights from Intellectual Property India

themes.title: Oil & Gas - gas economy (CGD/LNG) + refining/upstream
themes.need: India's gas-economy push now collides with an outright policy reversal. ATGL grew volume 13% to 303 MMSCM and revenue 27% to INR 1,908cr, yet EBITDA FELL sequentially to INR 281cr (~14.7% margin, from INR 310cr) because the government withdrew the pooled-gas mechanism after the West Asia 'peace deal', pushing ATGL to ~15% spot volumes with Brent above $107/bbl; management also noted NWG price is 12% of the Indian crude basket, so a 62% domestic mix protects far less than it looks, and CNG station adds slowed to +5 from +25 in Q4 even as CNG demand grows ~30%. The same shock ran the other way for integrated refining: RELIANCE delivered O2C EBITDA of INR 17,000cr (+17%) THROUGH the Strait-of-Hormuz closure at 96-97% throughput while Asian peers ran 15-20% below capacity, with ethane+ROGC at ~70% of ethylene feed as distillate cracks blew out (gas oil $16 to $63, ATF $14 to $62). MGL/GUJGASLTD/IGL/IRMENERGY carry the same CGD margin squeeze; PETRONET/OIL/ONGC/IOC ride LNG-infra + domestic-gas; CHENNPETRO/MRPL ride GRM cracks; DEEPINDS/JINDRILL/SEAMECLTD on ONGC E&P capex; AEGISLOG/AEGISVOPAK add LPG/gas terminalling.
themes.driver: Whether the pooled/APM gas-allocation mechanism is restored (the single biggest CGD earnings variable); LNG spot price and Brent; GRM/distillate cracks; ONGC rig tenders & day-rates.
